L31: # Coisotropic Hypersurfaces in Grassmannians
L32: 
L33: Kathlén Kohn Affiliation: Institute of Mathematics, Affiliation: TU Berlin, Germany Email: kohn@math.tu-berlin.de
L34: ###### Abstract
L35: To every projective variety $X$, we associate a list of hypersurfaces in different Grassmannians, called the coisotropic hypersurfaces of $X$. These include the Chow form and the Hurwitz form of $X$. Gel’fand, Kapranov and Zelevinsky characterized coisotropic hypersurfaces by a rank one condition on tangent spaces. We present a new and simplified proof of that result.
L36: We show that the coisotropic hypersurfaces of $X$ equal those of its projectively dual variety, and that their degrees are the polar degrees of $X$. Coisotropic hypersurfaces of Segre varieties are defined by hyperdeterminants, and all hyperdeterminants arise in that manner. We generalize Cayley’s differential characterization of coisotropy and derive new equations for the Cayley variety which parametrizes all coisotropic hypersurfaces of given degree in a fixed Grassmannian.
L37: We provide a Macaulay2 package for transitioning between $X$ and its coisotropic hypersurfaces.
L38: 
L39: Keywords: Chow form, hyperdeterminant, polar degree, associated hypersurface, Grassmannian, Macaulay2
L40: ## 1 Chow Forms, Hurwitz Forms and Beyond
L41: Historically one of the main motivations for the introduction of Chow forms was the parametrization of all subvarieties of $\mathbb{P}^{n}$ with fixed dimension and degree. The parametrization of 0-dimensional varieties is trivial, hypersurfaces can be parametrized by their defining equations, and linear subspaces are points in their respective Grassmannian. Hence, the first non-trivial case are curves in 3-space of degree (at least) two.
L42: Chow forms of space curves were first introduced by Cayley [cite18†Cay60 ]. The generalization to arbitrary varieties was given by Chow and van der Waerden [cite19†CvdW37 ]. For a given variety $X\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n}$ of dimension $k$, projective subspaces of dimension $n-k-1$ have typically no intersection with the variety, but those subspaces that do intersect $X$ form a hypersurface in the corresponding Grassmannian.
L43: The Chow form of $X$ is the defining polynomial of this hypersurface, which is a unique (up to scaling with constants) polynomial in the coordinate ring of the Grassmannian. It has the same degree as $X$ and determines $X$ uniquely.
L44: Consider now the same given variety $X$, but projective subspaces of dimension $n-k$. These are expected to have a finite number of intersection points with $X$, given by the degree $d$ of $X$. The subspaces which do not intersect $X$ in $d$ reduced points form again a hypersurface in the corresponding Grassmannian, as long as $d\geq 2$. The defining polynomial of this hypersurface is called Hurwitz form of $X$ [cite20†Stu17 ].
L45: Equivalently, this hypersurface is the Zariski closure of the set of all $(n-k)$-subspaces that intersect $X$ non-transversely at some smooth point. In this sense, it plays a crucial role in the study of the condition of intersecting a projective variety with varying linear subspaces [cite21†Bü17 ]. Moreover, Chow forms of curves and Hurwitz forms of surfaces in 3-space define exactly the self-dual hypersurfaces in the Grassmannian of lines in $\mathbb{P}^{3}$ [cite22†Cat14 ].
L46: A natural generalization of the above described hypersurfaces is studied in Chapters 3.3 and 4.3 of [cite23†GKZ94 ]: the $i$-th higher associated hypersurface of a variety $X\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n}$ of dimension $k$ is defined as the Zariski closure of the set of all $(n-k-1+i)$-dimensional subspaces that intersect $X$ at a smooth point non-transversely. This article is devoted to the study of these hypersurfaces. Our main contributions are the following.
L47: We state for which index $i$ the above definition yields indeed a hypersurface (Cor. cite24†6 ), and we show that the degrees of these hypersurfaces are the polar degrees of $X$ (Thm. cite25†9 ). We give a new proof for the main result in [cite23†GKZ94 ] about these hypersurfaces: the higher associated hypersurfaces are exactly the coisotropic hypersurfaces [cite23†GKZ94 , Ch. 4, Thm. 3.14], which are hypersurfaces in Grassmannians whose normal spaces at smooth points are spanned by homomorphisms of rank one.
L48: Note that the latter definition is independent of any underlying projective variety. The proof in [cite23†GKZ94 ] uses machinery from Lagrangian varieties to prove the existence of the projective variety $X$ a given coisotropic hypersurface is associated to, whereas our proof (Thm. cite26†14 ) is more direct and defines the underlying variety $X$ explicitly.
L49: Due to this result, we will use a more meaningful name for our main objects of study: in the following, the $i$-th higher associated hypersurface of $X$ is called the $i$-th coisotropic hypersurface of $X$. Furthermore, we derive that the coisotropic hypersurfaces of the projectively dual variety $X^{\vee}$ are the coisotropic hypersurfaces of $X$ in reversed order (Thm. cite27†20 ). Finally, we generalize Cayley’s [cite18†Cay60 ] differential characterization of coisotropy (Thm.
L50: cite28†31 ), and present a Macaulay2 [cite29†GS ] package for computations with coisotropic hypersurfaces (Sec. cite15†9 ).
L51: Coisotropic hypersurfaces have many applications in well-studied areas as well as recent research. As we will see in Section cite10†4 , coisotropic hypersurfaces are the analogue of polar varieties in Grassmannians. Hyperdeterminants are special cases of coisotropic hypersurfaces (see Sec. cite13†7 ). Moreover, coisotropic hypersurfaces and their (iterated) singular loci appear naturally in algebraic vision [cite30†KST ].
L52: The unitary group acts transitively on the tangent spaces of a coisotropic hypersurface, which allows to compute volumes of coisotropic hypersurfaces with the kinematic formula [cite31†BL ]. This is essential for the probabilistic Schubert calculus proposed in [cite31†BL ].
L53: Section cite9†3 shows that the coisotropic hypersurfaces of a projective variety are essentially projectively dual to the Segre product of the variety with projective spaces. With this, we determine for which indices $i$ the $i$-th coisotropic hypersurface has indeed codimension one in its ambient Grassmannian. We prove in Section cite10†4 that the degrees of the coisotropic hypersurfaces coincide with the polar degrees. Section cite11†5 revisits the main theorem of [cite23†GKZ94 ] about coisotropic hypersurfaces.
L54: The coisotropic hypersurfaces of a variety and its projectively dual will be related in Section cite12†6 . We discuss hyperdeterminants in Section cite13†7 . The Cayley variety – formed by all coisotropic hypersurfaces of fixed degree in a fixed Grassmannian – as well as characterizations for coisotropy in Plücker coordinates are studied in Section cite14†8 . Finally, we shortly describe our Macaulay2 package in Section cite15†9 .
L55: As a preparation, naming conventions for different coordinate systems of Grassmannians and some further basic notions will be introduced in the following section.
L56: ## 2 Preliminaries
L57: This article focuses on projective varieties over $\mathbb{C}$. Let $V$ be an $(n+1)$-dimensional complex vector space, and $\mathbb{P}(V)$ its projectivization. If $V=\mathbb{C}^{n+1}$, we will simply write $\mathbb{P}^{n}:=\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{C}^{n+1})$. By $\mathbb{P}(V)^{\ast}$ we denote the projectivization of the dual space $V^{\ast}$, which is formed by hyperplanes in $\mathbb{P}(V)$.
L58: The two projective spaces $\mathbb{P}(V)^{\ast}$ and $\mathbb{P}(V)$ can be identified by sending every point $y=(y_{0}:\ldots:y_{n})\in\mathbb{P}(V)$ to the hyperplane
L59:  | $\displaystyle\left\{y=0\right\}:=\left\{x\in\mathbb{P}(V)\;\middle|\;\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n}y_{i}x_{i}=0\right\}\in\mathbb{P}(V)^{\ast}.$  |  | (1)

L61: Throughout the rest of this article, let $X\subseteq\mathbb{P}(V)$ be an irreducible non-empty variety. We denote the set of smooth points of $X$ by $\mathrm{Reg}(X)$, and the embedded tangent space of $X$ at $x\in\mathrm{Reg}(X)$ by
L62:  | $\displaystyle T_{x}X:=\left\{y\in\mathbb{P}(V)\;\middle|\;\forall f\in I(X):\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n}\frac{\partial f}{\partial X_{i}}(x)\cdot y_{i}=0\right\},$  |
L63: where $I(X)\subseteq\mathbb{C}[X_{0},\ldots,X_{n}]$ denotes the vanishing ideal of $X$. A hyperplane in $\mathbb{P}(V)$ is called tangent to $X$ at a smooth point $x\in X$ if it contains $T_{x}X$. The Zariski closure $X^{\vee}$ in $\mathbb{P}(V)^{\ast}$ of the set of all hyperplanes that are tangent to $X$ at some smooth point is called the projectively dual variety of $X$. If $X$ is irreducible, so is $X^{\vee}$ [cite23†GKZ94 , Ch. 1, Prop. 1.3].
L64: We will make frequent use of the following biduality of projective varieties over $\mathbb{C}$, which is also known as reflexivity.
L65: ###### Theorem 1 ([cite23†GKZ94 , Ch. 1, Thm. 1.1]).
L66: 
L67: For every projective variety $X\subseteq\mathbb{P}(V)$, we have $(X^{\vee})^{\vee}=X$. More precisely, if $x\in\mathrm{Reg}(X)$ and $H\in\mathrm{Reg}(X^{\vee})$, then $H$ is tangent to $X$ at $x$ if and only if $x$ – regarded as a hyperplane in $\mathbb{P}(V)^{\ast}$ – is tangent to $X^{\vee}$ at $H$.
L68: The Grassmannian of all projective subspaces in $\mathbb{P}^{n}$ of dimension $l$ is denoted by $\mathrm{Gr}(l,\mathbb{P}^{n})$. For $0\leq i\leq k:=\dim(X)$ and a projective subspace $L\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n}$ of dimension $n-k+i-1$, the dimension of $L$ intersected with $T_{x}X$ equals $i-1$ for almost all $x\in X$. Those subspaces that have a larger intersection with some $T_{x}X$ (for $x\in\mathrm{Reg}(X)$) form a subvariety of the respective Grassmannian.
L69: ###### Definition 2.
L70: 
L71: For $i\in\{0,\ldots,k\}$, the $i$-th coisotropic variety of $X$ is defined as
L72: 
L73:  | $\displaystyle\mathrm{CH}_{i}(X):=\overline{\left\{L\mid\exists x\in\mathrm{Reg}(X)\cap L:\dim(L\cap T_{x}X)\geq i\right\}}\subseteq\mathrm{Gr}(n-k+i-1,\mathbb{P}^{n}).$  |
L74: 
L75: In [cite23†GKZ94 ] these varieties are called higher associated hypersurfaces (cf. Ch. 3, Sec. 2E and Ch. 4, Sec. 3). For $i=0$, the above definition reduces to the Chow hypersurface
L76:  | $\displaystyle\mathrm{CH}_{0}(X)=\left\{L\in\mathrm{Gr}(n-k-1,\mathbb{P}^{n})\mid X\cap L\neq\emptyset\right\}.$  |
L77: We will see in Corollary cite24†6 that $\mathrm{CH}_{0}(X)$ is indeed a hypersurface in $\mathrm{Gr}(n-k-1,\mathbb{P}^{n})$ for every $X$. Thus it is defined by one polynomial in the coordinate ring of $\mathrm{Gr}(n-k-1,\mathbb{P}^{n})$, which is unique up to a constant factor [cite23†GKZ94 , Ch. 3, Prop. 2.1], known as the Chow form of $X$. The case $i=1$ is studied in [cite20†Stu17 ].
L78: The variety $\mathrm{CH}_{1}(X)$ is a hypersurface if and only if $\deg(X)\geq 2$, and its corresponding polynomial in the coordinate ring of $\mathrm{Gr}(n-k,\mathbb{P}^{n})$ is called the Hurwitz form of $X$. For all $i$, the condition $\dim(L\cap T_{x}X)\geq i$ is equivalent to $\dim(L+T_{x}X)\leq n-1$, meaning that $L$ intersects $X$ at $x$ non-transversely.
L79: ### 2.1 Coordinate Systems
L80: 
L81: Different coordinates on Grassmannians are discussed in [cite23†GKZ94 , Ch. 3, Sec. 1]. We follow the conventions used in [cite20†Stu17 ]. There are six different ways of specifying a point $L\in\mathrm{Gr}(l,\mathbb{P}^{n})$, which we call primal/dual Plücker/Stiefel/affine coordinates.
L82: First, let $A\in\mathbb{C}^{(n-l)\times(n+1)}$ be such that $L$ is the projectivization of the kernel of $A$. The entries of $A$ are the primal Stiefel coordinates of $L$, and the maximal minors $p_{i_{1}\ldots i_{n-l}}$ of $A$ are the primal Plücker coordinates of $L$. Up to scaling, the Plücker coordinates are unique, whereas the Stiefel coordinates are clearly not: multiplying $A$ with any invertible $(n-l)\times(n-l)$ matrix does not change its kernel.
L83: Hence, when denoting by $S(n-l,n+1)$ the Stiefel variety of all complex $(n-l)\times(n+1)$ matrices of full rank, the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(l,\mathbb{P}^{n})$ can be seen as the quotient $S(n-l,n+1)/GL(n-l)$.
L84: Pick now a maximal linearly independent subset of columns of $A$, indexed by $\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{n-l}\}$, and multiply the inverse of this submatrix by $A$ itself. The resulting matrix has the same kernel as $A$ and its columns indexed by $\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{n-l}\}$ form the identity matrix. The remaining entries of this new matrix are the primal affine coordinates of $L$. These give a unique representation of $L$ in the primal affine chart

L124: ## 3 Cayley Trick
L125: 
L126: The Chow hypersurface can be constructed as the dual of a Segre product, which is known as the Cayley trick [cite23†GKZ94 , Ch. 3, Thm. 2.7]. We generalize this for all coisotropic varieties. Consider the Segre embedding

L128:  | $\displaystyle\left((\mathbb{P}^{k-i}\times X)^{\vee}\right)^{\ast}$  | $\displaystyle\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{C}^{(k-i+1)\times(n+1)}\right).$  |

L147: Now consider $\overline{p^{-1}(\mathrm{CH}_{i}(X))}$, which is the Zariski closure of the set of all full rank $A\in\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{C}^{(k-i+1)\times(n+1)})$ such that $\boldsymbol{x}\in\ker\boldsymbol{A}$ and $\dim(\ker(\boldsymbol{A})\cap T_{\boldsymbol{x}}\mathrm{cone}(X))\geq i+1$ for some $x\in\mathrm{Reg}(X)$. Hence, it is enough the show the following two equivalences:
L148:  | $\displaystyle\{\boldsymbol{A}=0\}\supseteq\mathbb{C}^{k-i+1}\otimes\boldsymbol{x}$  | $\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\boldsymbol{x}\in\ker\boldsymbol{A},$  |
L149:  | $\displaystyle\exists\boldsymbol{y}\in\mathbb{C}^{k-i+1}\setminus\{0\}:\{\boldsymbol{A}=0\}\supseteq\boldsymbol{y}\otimes T_{\boldsymbol{x}}\mathrm{cone}(X)$  | $\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\dim(\ker(\boldsymbol{A})\cap T_{\boldsymbol{x}}\mathrm{cone}(X))\geq i+1.$  |
